en: Preface:

To begin with, the merit of *prajñā* is inconceivable because it illuminates and shatters all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane realms, thereby penetratingly perceiving the source of nature.
Sentient beings, following along with ignorance, dwell long upon this shore, transmigrating through birth and death.
Death. The Bodhisattva, following in accordance with Prajñā, establishes himself upon the further shore and loftily realizes Nirvāṇa.
Indeed, Prajñā is the compassionate vessel for crossing the sea of suffering and the bright torch that dispels the long night. It is the teacher of all Buddhas and is venerated by all devas;
how could one not believe in it?
For twenty years, the World-Honored One, for the sake of his disciples, thoroughly investigated the two selves until he reached the three emptinesses directly;
he refined them with subtle discernment and extensively expounded upon Prajñā. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* consists of sixteen assemblies across four locations, totaling six hundred fascicles.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* is located in the second section, the ninth assembly, volume five hundred and seventy-seven.

Since its transmission to this land, there have been six translations in total; however, those currently revered and propagated all follow the version from the Qin dynasty. In India, there was the Bodhisattva Asaṅga.
Having attained the first bhūmi, he read this sutra but could not fathom its depths.
He then entered the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi* and ascended to Tuṣita Heaven, where he personally received from Maitreya the eighty-line verses used to explain this sutra.

He further transmitted these verses to his younger brother, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, each of whom composed a treatise to explain them. Vasubandhu’s commentary explained the text by resolving doubts and dispelling attachments.
The commentary was composed by the Tang dynasty Chan Master Zongmi of Mount Gui Peak, who extracted the essential points of the two treatises (*Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*).

He categorized the sūtra text according to Vasubandhu’s system, while his exegesis combined both Asaṅga and Vasubandhu. Furthermore, he consulted other treatises and compiled various commentaries, titling his work *Sūtra-lun-zuan-yao* (Essential Compendium of Sūtra and Treatise).
During the Song dynasty, the Dharma Master Zixuan of Changshui also produced the *Kanding ji* (Record of Collation and Determination).
I have explained this in seven fascicles. This *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is a branch of the True Source (*dharmadhātu*), transmitted through successive sages.
Tracing the current back to its source, Changshui followed Guifeng; Guifeng followed the two treatises; the two treatises followed Doushuai;

and Doushuai received it directly from Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*). Every word has its basis, and every character is without error—like using a family deed to manage one’s ancestral estate. Furthermore...
What cause for doubt is there? Later students settle for their own meager learning; there are those among the ancient commentaries and records who have never set eyes upon them in their entire lives.
Worse still, they indulge their own arbitrary views and hastily compose annotations. A discrepancy of even a hair’s breadth results in a chasm as vast as heaven and earth.
To mislead future generations, the harm is no small matter. During his leisure from meditative practice, the Dharma Master Hanhui took this sutra as his seal.

This is the luminous mirror of the mind. I have immersed myself in ancient commentaries and records for many years; however, their language is concise and archaic, making them difficult for beginners to access.
Therefore, I have excised the redundancies and extracted the essentials, further elaborating upon and clarifying them.

I have titled this work *Yangu* (Expounding the Ancients), so that readers may understand clearly upon opening the volume, awaken the four minds and give rise to the myriad practices, shatter all doubts, and penetrate the three emptinesses. Its...
The merit for those who study the *Prajñāpāramitā* is exceedingly great; therefore, I joyfully compose this preface to place at the beginning of the volumes.
Written on the third day after the Lantern Festival in the first month of the year of Bingchen by the Śramaṇa Daopai of Fusha.
Preface to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: Although there are many lay practitioners capable of reciting it, commentaries upon it are likewise numerous.

Yet, when it comes to the great purport of the *Prajñā*, not only do those who recite it remain bewildered, but even those who provide commentaries may not have fully grasped its meaning. Upon examining this...
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga had realized the first bhūmi; yet when he read this sūtra, he could not fathom its meaning.

Upon ascending to Tuṣita, he received the instructions of Maitreya, and subsequently transmitted them to Vasubandhu, who then began to compose treatises to explain it. Thus it was that Guifeng of the Tang dynasty...
The *Changshui* [Preface] of the Song dynasty traces the current back to its source, with each contributing its own insights;

yet all are refined and subtle in diction and meaning, such that they are difficult to comprehend without long-standing study. Thus, how easy would it be to speak of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*?

Ordinary people of this vast world, mired in ignorance, dullness, and darkness, drift up and down in the ocean of suffering; without *prajñā*, they cannot be ferried across. Yet, this cannot be achieved without first generating the bodhicitta within oneself.

How could one directly realize Prajñā? It is simply that people are unwilling to do so. Furthermore, the light of Prajñā wisdom illuminates and shatters all phenomena, penetrating thoroughly to the source of nature;
it not only sweeps away all mundane sentiments but also leaves no room for saintly conceptualizations.
Thus, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* takes non-abiding as its essence and the destruction of all things as its function. Those who recite or explain it fail to awaken to this.

The sublime purport [of this scripture] cannot be grasped by merely seeking its words; I fear it would lead one further away from the sutra itself. Since my youth, I have relied upon superior practitioners and have delighted in hearing the *Vajracchedikā* recited.
Now that I have recovered from a severe illness, I realize that life and death are not permanent, which serves as a profound admonition to spur me on.
I now hope to focus my mind single-mindedly on the Jewel of the Dharma and fathom its profound depths. It happened that Master Hanhui of Chan showed me an ancient commentary on the *Vajracchedikā*.
As for the "Exposition of the Ancients," it comprises the two treatises (*śāstras*), as well as the *Zuanyao*, *Kanding*, and other such works.

It elucidates and clarifies these texts, revealing the secrets that previous sages had not fully exhausted, thereby constituting a comprehensive commentary. Within it, the narrative is lucid and the phrasing concise; its principles are profound while its expression is clear and accessible.
The moment one opens and examines it, the ice of one's thoughts melts away. Looking at those who write commentaries, each has established their own distinct school of thought;

yet the Master alone calls his work a "Commentary on the Ancients" (*Yangu*). This is precisely because when the Master annotates a sutra, he does not establish his own independent interpretations, but returns the commentary back to the ancients—thus, the method of annotation itself is not fixed.
From this, we know that the treatises and commentaries of the sages and worthies of the past were themselves the very methods of treatise and commentary.
Nor is it established. It is through this that one is liberated. When the Tathāgata extensively expounds the Prajñā, even the dharma of Prajñā itself is not established.

Taking the ancient teachings as a basis and summarizing the meaning of the sūtras, its benefit in inspiring the four minds, realizing the three emptinesses, dispelling all doubts, and adorning the myriad practices—how could such merit be slight? Wherever this book resides, one should pay homage and circumambulate it.
Circumambulate [the site] and scatter various flowers and incense upon it.
Written as a postscript by Fan Yin of Kuaiji, with respectful greetings.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is the secret essential for the transmission of the mind from Buddha to Patriarch.
By taking the donning of robes and holding of the alms bowl as its introductory theme, it seeks to show that *prajñā* is not separate from the midst of daily life.

Although it refutes appearances and severs doubts therein, neither the practice of phenomena nor the contemplation of principle has ever been neglected. Its saving of sentient beings is without a savior; it gives rise to non-abiding.
With a mind free from selfhood and so forth, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas; that which is not adornment is called adornment, and so on.
Such categories are all correctly and partially interchanged, avoiding sharp edges while remaining subtle and luminous—this depends upon the person.

Thus, Huangmei used this to seal the mind, and Zengxi heard it and attained awakening; how could this have been in vain? However, the meaning and intent of this sutra are profound and far-reaching. Ancient...

Now, as for the commentaries, they number nearly a hundred schools. Only those of Vasubandhu and Asanga from India West, who received the lineage from Maitreya, established eighteen stages of abiding to secretly reveal the gradations of progress and severed twenty-seven doubts, thereby secretly connecting the vital currents [of the Dharma] in perfect accord with the intent of the World-Honored One’s formless Mahāyāna.
In this land [of China], there were [commentaries by] Qinglong, Dayun, Zisheng, and Chenwai.
The various commentaries either follow or contradict one another, leaving scholars without a means of arbitration.

During the mid-Tang dynasty, the Chan Master Zongmi of Guifeng made a prescient judgment based on Asanga’s sevenfold categories of meaning and provided a structural analysis based on Vasubandhu’s *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exposition of the Treatise) concerning the resolution of doubts.
He further collected various commentaries and titled his work *Sūtra-śāstra-zǎnyào* (Essential Compendium of Commentaries and Treatises).

He also composed the *Jìlüè* (Brief Record) as an exposition, which accorded with the imperial intent above and adapted to the capacities of the multitude below; he was truly a master of the Dharma in this age of semblance images.

During the Five Dynasties, Master Shíbi of the Stone Wall Monastery adopted the *Jìlüè* and separately produced the *Guǎnglù* (Extended Record). Its language was sometimes prolix and lengthy, causing scholars much hardship. During the Tiānshèng era of the Great Song dynasty, Cháng...
The Dharma Master Shuǎn of Shuǐzǐ further revised and edited [the text], pruning the cumbersome and excising the redundant, while rejecting the spurious to preserve the authentic.

He titled it the *Kāndìngjì* (Record of Collated Determination). Truly, he may be called a meritorious minister of the Inner Court and a true descendant of Guishan. Thus, these sacred texts have not fallen into ruin.
His merit is truly great! In the summer of the Jǐyǒu year, I was honored to join the pure assembly at the Shígǔ "Field for Selecting Buddhas.
There, together with my friends, we deliberated upon its general meaning. During my mountain retreats, when the days were long, I occasionally consulted it;

however, while the *Zuǎnyào* (Compendium of Essentials) is concise and ancient, it is difficult to penetrate, and the *Kāndìng* (Collated Determination) is so detailed that one cannot remember it all. Therefore, I have combined these two sections and deleted the redundancies.
Taking the essentials and harmonizing them, I have elaborated upon and analyzed the contents therein so as not to contradict the intent of the ancient masters.
I have humbly titled this work *Yangu* (Expounding the Ancients), intending it merely as a personal aid against forgetfulness for my daily study and reflection.
It truly serves as a guide for awakening the four minds, practicing the six perfections, shattering the two selves, and penetrating the three emptinesses. At that time...
Written in the autumn of the Jiyou year, on the day after the full moon of the ninth month, by the junior scholar Jiyen at the Stone Drum Chan Monastery (Xuanfochang), the site for selecting buddhas.
An Exposition of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* based on the ancients,
composed by the junior scholar Śramaṇa Jiyen of Jin’an.
In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "vajra" refers to a celestial treasure possessed by Śakra. Those with meager merit find it difficult to behold.
It possesses the three meanings of being firm, sharp, and luminous. Its substance is extremely firm; no object can destroy it. Its function is extremely sharp; it can destroy...
All things have characteristics that are extremely luminous and capable of illuminating everything. Thus, the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra* states:
"Just as Śakra’s vajra-jewel can destroy the asuras, so too does wisdom shatter the mountain of afflictions.
Therefore, the Buddha used this as a metaphor for the three types of *prajñā*. In the Sanskrit language, *prajñā* is translated here as "wisdom. Its...

The essence is precisely the *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). It is the fundamental nature inherently possessed by us, eternally real and pure, remaining constant throughout past and present.
Although it has undergone the cycle of birth and death for many kalpas, it has never been diminished; this is the meaning of its ultimate solidity.
Its function is precisely the contemplative illumination of *prajñā*. It is also the light of the mind that has been present from the beginning;

it may remain unmanifest, or it may manifest, whereby it is able to sever delusions and attachments. Since beginningless time, there is no ignorance or affliction (*kleśa*) that it does not destroy. This is the meaning of "extremely sharp.
In terms of its functional capacity, it is called a *pāramitā*, which here means "reaching the other shore," signifying that one rides upon the boat of *prajñā*.
The vessel sails away from this shore of birth and death, crosses the turbulent middle stream of afflictions, and reaches the further shore of nirvāṇa.

Nirvāṇa is translated here as "perfect stillness" (yuánjì) and is also called "extinction and deliverance" (mièdù). All sentient beings are already in the state of quiescent extinction; they do not need to undergo further extinction.

It is only because of delusion and inversion that one falsely perceives birth and death as being "on this shore. If one awakens to the fact that birth and death are fundamentally empty and have always been perfect stillness (*parinirvāṇa*), this is called "reaching the other shore.
If the phrase *prajñā* (wisdom) is included and the characters are transposed, it should be read as "the wisdom that reaches the other shore."
The first seven characters are that which is explained (*vācya*); the character "sūtra" (*sūtra*) is that which explains (*vācaka*). It possesses four meanings:

penetration (*anubandha*), collection (*saṃgraha*), and permanence (*nitya*). "Penetration" means like a thread passing through flowers; it refers to the threading together of the meanings that ought to be known. "Collection" means like warp threads being held by weft;

it refers to the gathering and sustaining of the sentient beings to be converted. "Permanence" means the sense of being unchanging; it is the unchanging [nature] of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The "Constant Way" (常道) refers to the meaning of "Dharma" as a guiding principle; it is the correct standard universally followed by Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions.
This is precisely the *prajñā* of words and letters (*nāma-prajñā*), which carries the sense of ultimate clarity.

If a student can, through the *prajñā* of words and letters, give rise to contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā*), and through the *prajñā* of contemplative illumination, realize the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), this is called the adamantine wisdom reaching the other shore (*pāramitā*).
Furthermore, the main text of the sutra’s commentary follows the conventional threefold division: the Introduction (Nidāna), the Main Body (Prakaraṇa), and the Dissemination (Parīndanā).

This is because when the World-Honored One was about to expound the Prajñā, he first manifested the causes and conditions; hence it is called the "Introduction Section. Once the causes and conditions were manifested, those present who were ready to receive the Dharma did so.
The essential purport of the entire scripture is set forth through its exposition and practice; therefore, it is called the "Correct Teaching" (Zhengzong).

Once the core purpose is clarified, one must strive for enlightenment and salvation, benefiting the present generation in the near term and future generations in the long term, so that its fragrance may be transmitted through the ages and the life-force of wisdom remains unbroken;
therefore, it is called "Circulation" (Liutong).

I. The Introductory Section. This section distinguishes between the "Certification of Faith" (*śraddhā-prasāda*) and the "Initiation" (*nidāna*). Herein lies the Certification of Faith, which consists of six elements of accomplishment:
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
Thus it is. This is the fulfillment of faith. When faith exists, the principles of what is spoken accord with reality; when they accord, the way of teacher and disciple is perfected.
In the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma, faith is that which enables entry, and wisdom is that which enables crossing over. Therefore, faith is placed at the beginning. Thus have I heard.
"Having heard" (*śruta*) refers to accomplishment. "I" (*aham*) is Ānanda’s own designation;

however, it is a conventional designation following worldly usage and is not the same as the "self" (*ātman*) imagined by ordinary people or non-Buddhists. "Having heard" means hearing directly from the source, not through hearsay.
If this Dharma were not established through sound and hearing, how could the teaching be founded? As for "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*):
This is the fulfillment of the timing. Even in worldly affairs, where people gather together, one must still await a period of prosperity.

How much more so for the great Dharma’s broad proclamation—how could it fail to coincide with such a fortunate destiny? Therefore, it is said that this is the time of a "Fortunate Assembly," when the Dharma King inaugurates his era.

Nevertheless, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, among devas and humans, the temporal divisions differ; here, we simply take the moment when the teacher and disciple are in accord and the teaching and listening reach their ultimate conclusion.

Therefore, it is said: "At one time. As for "Buddha," it signifies the master of accomplishment. In the Sanskrit language, it is fully called *Buddhaya*; here it is translated as "The Awakened One" (*Buddha*).
It possesses the threefold meaning of self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of awakening; thus, he is called a Buddha.

This refers to our original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, who is the master of this teaching. Were it not for one of Great Awakening, who could have expounded such a Great Dharma? [End of] Chapter on the Preface.
“Vaishali and so forth” refers to the accomplishment of the location. “Shravasti” is the Sanskrit term; here it is translated as “Renowned for Wealth.
Because its people and resources were so prosperous that they were heard of throughout the Five Indias, this was the place where the Dharma was preached.
It is located in Central India, in the kingdom where King Prasenajit resided. Approximately five *li* to the southeast outside the city was the garden of Prince Jeta. Great...
Your servant Sudatta—here translated as "Good Giver"—constantly provided relief to the impoverished people of the kingdom; thus, people called him the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada.
He purchased a grove by spreading gold and the Prince relinquished the trees, together constructing a vihāra and inviting the Buddha to preach the Dharma.
One may thereby perceive the Great Dharma of Prajñā; it could not have been proclaimed in a place other than this sacred site. Together with the Great...
“Bhikṣu-saṃgha” refers to the perfection of the assembly. If there were no one in the assembly capable of understanding, for whom would I preach?
Now, those with the capacity for spiritual resonance fill the space before me; I cannot but speak. The term “bhikṣu” contains three meanings: first, the mendicant (yācanaka).

This means that above, he begs for the Dharma to sustain his life of wisdom, and below, he begs for food to nourish his physical body. It is also called "the destroyer of evil" (pāpahara) and "the terrifier of Māra" (mārakampana).
"Great" means numerous; it signifies weightiness in number and loftiness in virtue.

For example, Kauṇḍinya, the three Kāśyapas, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, the householder Yaśas, and their retinues were all together at one time and in one place, harmoniously assembled and listening in great numbers.
This may truly be called magnificent. Yet, these individuals had all previously served non-Buddhist paths with difficulty.
For many years he labored in vain without attaining any realization; yet as soon as he beheld the Buddha, he immediately ascended to the fruit of sainthood.
Moved by the profound kindness of the Buddha, he constantly attended upon him as a personal attendant; for this reason, his name is listed specifically among the retinue.

As for the other members of the eight classes of supernatural beings and the fourfold assembly, they are all included within the section on the dissemination of the teaching. To list them from beginning to end would be merely a matter of abbreviation.
At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

Having gone through the city begging for food in due order, he returned to his original place. When he had finished eating, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat, and sat down.

This is the introductory sequence. As the Prajñāpāramitā is about to be expounded, the act of donning robes and holding an alms bowl is used as the introduction to demonstrate that Prajñā is not separate from the midst of daily life.
"At that time" refers to the moment when the great assembly had gathered like clouds.
As for the time of eating, it is between the hours of the Dragon (7–9 a.m. and the Snake (9–11 a.m.).

Our Śākyamuni World-Honored One, having manifested his appearance among humans and demonstrated conformity with human laws, likewise at the time of eating, donned his saṃghāṭī robe, held his dark-blue lapis lazuli bowl, and, with dignified and orderly deportment and solemn, respectful adherence to the Dharma, departed from Jetavana and entered Śrāvastī, personally following the example of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Regarding the method of begging for alms: internally, one realizes the principle of equality; externally, one empties the distinction between the poor and the wealthy.
Therefore, within the city, regardless of whether a place is pure or impure, and without discriminating between the noble and the lowly, one begs in successive order.

Since the Buddha’s mind is equal, it causes the merit obtained by the donor to be equal as well. Having received food, one again exits the great city and returns to the original location. The original location...
As for the facts, they concern the Jetavana Vihāra; as for the principle, it concerns the true mark of ultimate emptiness. Whatever food the Buddha obtained, he divided it into four portions:
first, he gave to his fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring; second, he bestowed upon the poor and the sick who begged;
third, he gave to sentient beings of water and land; fourth, he ate himself. Having finished eating, he would then gather up his robe and bowl and wash his feet. Thus it is said in the Āgamas.

The Sūtra states: "When the Buddha walks, he remains four finger-widths above the ground, and lotus flowers receive his feet. As for his washing his feet now: previously, when walking out to beg for alms, he would go barefoot;
upon returning, he would wash away the dust and filth as a model for future generations. Regarding his spreading out a seat and sitting: [the text continues].
The attendant prepared the seat for him, yet he spoke only of Prajñāpāramitā. The Buddha himself prepared the seat because he held Prajñāpāramitā in the highest respect.
Donning his robes and taking up his bowl symbolized *śīla* (morality); spreading the mat and sitting down symbolized *samādhi* (concentration).

By means of *śīla* and *samādhi*, he gave rise to *prajñā*, causing people to contemplate the elephant and realize its meaning. Thus, this act of donning the robes, taking up the bowl, washing the feet, and spreading the mat [is the preparation for] Prajñāpāramitā.

If it were the true mechanism [of the Dharma], it would have already been revealed without remainder. Thus, Subhūti did not wait for the Tathāgata to open his mouth before exclaiming how rare and marvelous it was;
this is much like the occasion at Vulture Peak when the Buddha held up a flower and Kāśyapa smiled. These two understood each other’s minds through silent recognition.
It is identical throughout; let the reader examine this in detail. The preceding section on the Introduction is concluded.
II. The Main Body of the Teaching.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti, being in the midst of the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and placed his right knee [on the ground].
He descended to the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; the Tathāgata well entrusts all bodhisattvas. World-Honored One, how should a good man or a good woman who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their minds?"
This was Subhūti’s formal request. A great bell suspended upon its frame does not ring without being struck; likewise, the Dharma-gift is not withheld, yet it is spoken only in response to inquiry.
Thus, within this single assembly at Jetavana, all present possess a mind that delights in the Dharma, yet none dared to venture a private request.

At that time, there was an elder of great virtue named Subhūti—here translated as "Born of Emptiness" (Kōshō) and also called "Well-Appeared" (Zen-gen)—who was foremost in the understanding of emptiness.
While the Tathāgata was putting on his robes, holding his bowl, and arranging his seat to sit, Subhūti suddenly realized the essence of the *prajñā* mind.
Thereupon, knowing the opportune moment and the proper time, he rose from his seat of dharma-emptiness.
Regarding the application of compassion and wisdom: baring the right shoulder and bending the right knee—both are specified as "right" to signify conformity to the Way.
Joining the palms signifies that wisdom merges with principle. The above constitutes the compiler’s description of the ritual for requesting the Dharma;
below follows Subhūti’s praise and request. First, he offers praise: although others do not know the sublime state of the Tathāgata’s daily activities, Śūnyatā-janman (Subhūti) [perceives it].

He alone knew this, and thus praised it as rare, saying: "Indeed, it is difficult to encounter even in vast kalpas; throughout the great trichiliocosm, there is but one such instance—how could it be found often?

As for "skillfully protecting and mindful of," this means that with great compassion, he protects and is mindful of those bodhisattvas whose faculties are mature, namely those from the third stage of the Three Sages upward.
This "protecting and being mindful" is to bestow empowerment and provide strength; by granting the power of fundamental wisdom, he causes them to achieve accomplishment.
The Buddha-dharma and the power of subsequently attained wisdom enable the transformation and instruction of sentient beings. Regarding "skillful entrustment":

through great compassion, those whose faculties are not yet mature are entrusted [to others], while those who have already attained the Mahāyāna are made not to abandon it, and those who have not yet attained the Mahāyāna are caused to advance further.
Thus, Maitreya’s verse says: "One should know the meaning of skillful protection; one bestows [this] upon their person."

To practice together, not to regress, and to attain what has not yet been attained—this is called "entrusting well. Regarding the subsequent request: the causal stage of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching consists of three layers.
First is the realization of one's original nature; second is the arousal of the bodhicitta; and third is the cultivation of the bodhisattva practices.
Therefore, in the *Avataṃsaka*, Sudhana first declares what he has already aroused before inquiring about the gates of practice; this sutra likewise emphasizes this point entirely.
Regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta: because this is the root of all practice, when Śūnyatā-janman (Empty-Born) realized this mind, he requested the method for authentic cultivation.

He did not do so merely for himself, but also on behalf of all sentient beings, petitioning that if a person does not arouse the mundane mind of humans and devas, nor the supramundane minds of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they should instead arouse [the bodhicitta].
The mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is extremely difficult to attain;

once one has entered into the protective mindfulness and entrustment of the Tathāgata, how could one not be taught the methods of practice? I venture to ask: previously, before you had resolved to attain enlightenment, [what was it like?]
While dwelling within the realms of the six sense objects, now that you have resolved to attain enlightenment, upon what ground should you establish yourself?

Previously, before you resolved to attain enlightenment, you followed after deluded thoughts; now that you have resolved to attain enlightenment, when such deluded thoughts arise, how should they be subdued?

I truly hope the Tathāgata will provide instruction so that you may know where to abide and how to subdue [the mind], thereby ensuring that your practice does not go astray and that you do not fall into further delusion.
This is the bodhicitta. This single question is the key to this entire sutra. According to the Wei translation, there are three questions: "How should one dwell? How should one practice?

How should one subdue the mind? The Buddha’s answer was to cause one to dwell securely in the four immeasurable minds, to cultivate the practices of the six pāramitās, and not to become attached to signs—this is the meaning of "subduing. The Qin translation omits the section on practice.
This means that dwelling in the Way and subduing the mind is itself the practice; one must not depart from this to seek a separate cultivation.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and mindfully sustains all bodhisattvas."
[Sakyamuni] said: "Excellent! I have entrusted this to you, O Bodhisattvas. Now listen attentively; I shall explain it for you.
Sons of good family and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide in this manner and subdue their minds in this manner.
[The assembly] replied: "So be it, World-Honored One. We wish to hear it with joy."

The repetition of "Excellent! (*sādhu*) is a praise for his inquiry; because Subhūti’s request was so skillfully made that it perfectly accords with the Buddha’s mind, the Buddha confirms it by saying:
"Subhūti," followed by two phrases which restate what he has been praised for, and then two phrases beginning with "You should now listen attentively."
He cautioned them to listen and granted permission to speak. What did he say? He spoke of the method for one who has generated the bodhicitta to abide in this way and to subdue the mind in this way;
this refers to the passage provided as the answer below. Furthermore, the two characters "in this way" (rúshì) point directly and straightforwardly to the truth:
if one does not abide in this way, then one is not abiding; if one does not subdue [the mind] in this way, then it is not subdued.
It transforms into the deluded mind; how, then, could one possibly attain unsurpassed bodhi? At that time, Śūnyatā-utpanna (Kōshō), having heard the teaching, responded with "Yes" (*ei*).

This is a term signifying comprehension, just as when Zeng Can heard the Way of the Single Thread and responded with "Yes," his mind was already clearly resolved and free from obstruction. Yet he further said, "I wish to hear it with joy."
This was indeed undertaken for the sake of the multitude.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this way:
'Whatever classes of sentient beings there may be—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether they possess..."

Whether they have form or are formless; whether they have perception, or lack perception, or have neither perception nor non-perception—I cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation.

Although in this way I liberate immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, in reality there is no sentient being who has been liberated. Why is that? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses a self...
The mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span—these are not a bodhisattva.
This is the Tathāgata’s direct answer to the question. Second: first, the answer to the question regarding abiding and subduing the mind.

This means that one should abide in the four [immeasurable] minds and subdue the mind that conceives of a self while saving sentient beings. Although there are two questions, the answers mutually clarify them.
Therefore, it first sets forth "subduing the mind" and later concludes with "abiding as instructed.

Guifeng, following the Wei translation, takes the three questions to present "subduing" as the general principle and "abiding in practice" as the specific application. However, upon examining the sutra text, there is no separate response regarding subduing;
thus, we know that subduing is contained within abiding in practice, wherein all things are made free from signs—this is the answer to subduing the mind.
Question: Therefore, by subduing [the afflictions], one gathers and abides in peace.

As to the previous question regarding "good sons and good daughters," the present answer states "bodhisattvas" because they have already resolved upon the Great Mind (mahācitta) and thus receive the title of bodhisattva. Bodhisattva...
This is translated as "Awakened Being" (Bodhisattva). It means that through wisdom one seeks the path of awakening above, and through compassion one transforms sentient beings below.
"Mahāsattva" is translated as "Sentient Beings of the Great Path-Mind.
"One should thus subdue the mind" refers to abiding in the four minds mentioned below, practicing the six perfections, and subduing the mind that clings to signs. [To] generate...

Regarding the bodhicitta, making the liberation of sentient beings one’s urgent task is its primary duty; all categories of sentient beings whatsoever must be delivered and liberated—this is the general description.
As for those born from eggs and so forth, this refers to the distinctions in modes of birth: gods and hell-beings are born by transformation (*aupapāduka*);
hungry ghosts admit of both womb-birth and transformation-birth; humans and animals each have all four; and there are various other subtle [beings], such as those born from water.
Regarding movement by land and air, it is impossible to fully enumerate their categories; however, speaking in terms of the distinctions of their bases (*āśraya*):

those with form consist of the four dhyānas, taking the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as their body; those without form consist of the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), taking the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-, saṃjñā-, saṃskāra-, vijñānaskandha*) as their body.
"Base" here carries the meaning of "body. Speaking in terms of the distinctions of their objects (*viṣaya*): those with perception are the formless [attainments].
Within the realms, there are two heavens: the Heaven of Infinite Space and the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness.
The "unconscious" refers to the Heaven of Nothingness. The "neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving" refers to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
In this way, the three realms are encompassed without exception. Those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta must surely deliver all beings until none remain. Therefore...
The *Maitreya-stotra* says: "Vast, foremost, and eternal; with a mind free from inversion, abiding in a profound resolve for the benefit [of others]—the merits of this vehicle are fulfilled.
To deliver all sentient beings throughout the triple world is to abide in the vast mind.
He causes all to enter the Tathāgata’s ultimate *nirvāṇa* without remainder and brings them to liberation. This is the first stage of mind (*citta*).
"Bringing immeasurable beings to liberation" reiterates the aforementioned distinction of taking birth. "Incalculable" reiterates the aforementioned distinction of the basis of reliance.
"Boundless" reiterates the aforementioned distinction of the sphere of activity. "No sentient beings [attain... [is stated].
Regarding "nirvāṇa" (extinction): if one perceives that there are sentient beings who can be saved, one retains the mark of saving beings and will inevitably give rise to weariness;

thus, one cannot save them constantly. One must know that because the nature of sentient beings is empty, because they share the same essence, this is the mark of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).
It does not require further extinction, for it is free from conceptualization and is the *dharmadhātu*. Therefore, it is said: "In truth, there are no sentient beings."

Regarding those who attain extinction (*nirvāṇa*), the *Śāstra* states: "In the equal and true Dharma-realm, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings. This refers to abiding in the mind of permanence.
As for the question "Why is this so?", the intent of the inquiry is: since he has indeed delivered sentient beings, why is it said that there is no delivering?
Why is this? It is because if one perceives that there are sentient beings who can be delivered, then one perceives a self as the deliverer.
If one perceives a self, then one possesses the four marks of person, sentient being, life-span, and individual—what difference is there between such a person and an inverted, ordinary worldling?
Conversely, it is revealed that in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa; thus, there are no four marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span. This is abiding.
It is the non-perverted mind. Master Dazhu said: "The nine classes of sentient beings are fully present within a single mind;
they are formed as they act. Therefore, ignorance constitutes egg-birth; being enveloped by afflictions constitutes womb-birth; being moistened by the waters of craving constitutes moisture-birth;
and the sudden arising of afflictions constitutes transformation-birth. Awakening is the Buddha; delusion is called [sentient being]."
Sentient beings: the Bodhisattva takes each and every thought-moment as sentient beings. If one realizes that the essence of each thought-moment is empty, this is called "delivering sentient beings.
The wise deliver those who have not yet taken form from the perspective of their own primordial limit (*mūla-koṭi*).
Since that which has not yet taken form is empty, they know that in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on anything regarding phenomena. That is to say, one should not dwell on form when practicing giving;
one should not dwell on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects when practicing giving.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give in this manner, without dwelling on signs. Why is that? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, their merit...
The merit is inconceivable. Subhūti, what do you think? Can the space of the eastern direction be measured?
"No, World-Honored One. Subhūti, can the space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured?
"No, World-Honored One. Subhūti, the merit of a bodhisattva who practices giving without dwelling on signs is likewise [inconceivable].
This is inconceivable, Subhūti. A bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed.
This second answer concerns the practice of subduing the mind; that is, practicing the six perfections without abiding in signs, thereby subduing the mind that grasps at signs.
As for what is called "not abiding in signs," it does not mean to extinguish signs so that they no longer exist; rather, it is because signs are fundamentally...
There is none. The mind does not dwell in attachment. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Ordinary beings perceive all phenomena merely as they follow after appearances;
failing to understand that phenomena are signless, they do not see the Buddha. Thus, non-attachment to appearances is the method for subduing the mind.

This must be clarified by way of practice. Regarding "in the Dharma," this is a general designation for all dharmas. "Should not be inferior" and so forth correctly clarifies the cultivation of practice.
Now, although practice comprises the six perfections, the term "generosity" (dāna) alone is used because generosity encompasses and subsumes all six perfections.

Therefore, Maitreya’s verse states: "The meaning of *dāna* (generosity) encompasses six: material gifts, fearlessness, and the Dharma; among these, one, two, and three are called the stages of cultivation.

This verse subsumes the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) within the three types of giving: material gifts encompass *dāna*; fearlessness encompasses ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*);
and the Dharma encompasses diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). That is to say, one [type of giving] corresponds to one [perfection], while two...

The two are subsumed [in one], and the three are subsumed in three; this is it. As for what is called "non-abiding," it means not abiding in the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), nor even in the fruit of Buddhahood or *bodhi*.
Among the eighty-one categories [of phenomena], none should be clung to or adhered to. Now, by mentioning only the six sense-objects, one is cited to represent them all.
Why is this so? The intent of this inquiry is to say: although the act of giving is uniform, if one abides in the mark of appearance (*nimitta*)...
What is inferior? Not abiding in signs is what is superior. The commentary states: Merit associated with signs is small; merit without signs is great.

If a bodhisattva is able to use the true wisdom of *prajñā* to illuminate and shatter illusory appearances while practicing generosity and cultivating the six perfections, the resulting merit will almost certainly transcend the bounds of ordinary perception and cannot be grasped.
This is because it is inconceivable. Therefore, the vast and inexhaustible emptiness of the ten directions is cited as a metaphor for it.

"One should simply abide as instructed" summarizes the question; that is to say, one should simply practice the six perfections without the mark of abiding, as taught by me—this is the place of abiding. This is to abide in non-abiding.

This concludes the section on "Abiding. In the preceding response to Subhūti’s direct question, it was stated that those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta should abide in the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), cultivate the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and thereby subdue the mind that clings to a self (*ātman*).

Thus, the main body of the teaching (*mūla-prakaraṇa*) is complete, and one may now enter the section on the dissemination of the Dharma (*parivarta*). Fearing that future students of Prajñāpāramitā might harbor doubts regarding the Tathāgata’s response, [the following is provided].
Therefore, following the traces of the preceding discourse, it was provisionally initiated by Subhūti to sever those doubts;
as these were successively produced one after another, there resulted twenty-seven sections. Thus, the verse of Maitreya says:
"In the matter of taming them, one distances oneself from the mind that grasps at signs, severs various doubts, and likewise prevents the arising of [conceptual] minds. This is what is meant.
First, a doubt arises: "The original purpose of practicing giving was to seek the fruit of Buddhahood; this is precisely abiding in the characteristics of the Buddha one seeks.
How can it be 'non-abiding'? Furthermore, taking 'formlessness' as the cause while seeking the fruit of Buddhahood with its thirty-two marks—would not cause and effect then be dissimilar?
This doubt follows from the preceding passage on "giving without abiding in appearances," as [the opponent] relies on...
Hearing that people take the physical marks and signs of a sixteen-foot-tall form as the Buddha, they do not know that the signless Dharma-body is the true Buddha;
therefore, the preceding dialogue concerning the cause of doubt arising from dwelling upon signs is presented in order to eliminate and sever it.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of physical marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of physical marks. Why is this? The physical marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are, in fact, not physical marks.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever marks there may be, they are all false and illusory. If one sees that all marks are non-marks,"
He then beheld the Tathāgata.
This [passage] severs the doubt regarding abiding in the marks while practicing giving with the aim of seeking Buddhahood.

Since Subhūti had doubted that one could seek the fruit of the thirty-two marks of a Buddha by taking formlessness as the cause, [the Buddha] therefore questioned him in return, saying: "What do you think?"
He reflected: "Can the Dharma-body Tathāgata be seen through the physical marks of a sixteen-foot body?
As soon as Śūnyatā-utpanna received this compassionate inquiry, he grasped the Buddha’s intention and replied: "No, World-Honored One. Such is the sharpness of a true monk.
A single stroke turns it; all that follows is modeled after this. Furthermore, he explains by means of self-inquiry:

"The reason one cannot see the Tathāgata through physical marks (lakṣaṇa) is that the six-foot body-mark is merely a reflection manifested by the Wisdom of Equality (samatājñāna) in response to the capacities of beings.
Like the moon in water, it appears to exist but is not real. How could it be the true Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata?"
"It is so. For the Dharma-body is unconditioned and does not fall into any numerical categories; therefore, it cannot be sought by grasping at signs.
Since Śūnyatā-utpanna had understood this principle, the Buddha then confirmed and expanded upon it, saying:
'Not only is the Buddha’s body signless, but all conditioned phenomena—whether the environment or its inhabitants, whether mundane or transcendent—are entirely illusory.'"
Because they are manifested from deluded thoughts, and since deluded thoughts are fundamentally empty, how could that which is manifested be real?
The two phrases "if one sees various marks" serve to preclude the practice of viewing emptiness by detaching from form.

Fearing that upon hearing that marks are illusory, one might separately seek a markless Buddha-body, it is said that "marks are themselves non-marks. If one sees what is non-mark, one sees the Dharmakāya Tathāgata. Why is this so?

This is because appearances are fundamentally exhausted by nature, and reality is fundamentally manifest by nature. Indeed, one who has resolved to attain enlightenment (bodhicitta) should not practice giving while dwelling upon appearances.

Regarding the second doubt: Subhūti, having heard the preceding two sections—that giving is practiced without dwelling (the profundity of the cause) and that the Buddha is seen without signs (the profundity of the fruit)—genuinely fears that in future ages it will be difficult for people to give rise to faith in this most profound principle;
he thus wonders what benefit there would be in speaking of it in vain. This section clearly expresses words of doubt, serving as a preliminary objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) to what follows.
"It is not so. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases, will give rise to true faith?
The Buddha told Subhūti, "Do not speak thus. After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, during the final five hundred years..."
Furthermore, Subhūti, there may be those who observe the precepts and cultivate merit who are able to give rise to faith in these words and take them as true.
You should know that such persons have not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas;

rather, they have already planted various roots of goodness in the presence of immeasurable thousands of millions of Buddhas. Upon hearing these words, they will give rise to pure faith for even a single thought-moment.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees all these sentient beings who shall obtain such immeasurable merit.

This refers to those who have severed both cause and effect, whose lack of faith and doubt are profound. The text has three parts: first, presenting the doubt regarding the absence of faith. [End of section on Emptiness.]
Jātiśroṇa heard that both the cause and the fruit were profound, and considering this to be a teaching difficult to believe, he suspected that there would be no one in the world who could have faith.
Second, [the Buddha] rebuked his doubt to manifest the nature of true faith. The Buddha, because of this, rebuked and stopped him, saying:
"Do not make such a statement that there is no genuine faith. Not only while the Tathāgata is in the world, but even after the Tathāgata has passed away, during the final five hundred years..."
In this age when strife is persistent, we are increasingly distant from the Sage and our spiritual faculties are increasingly inferior.
Nevertheless, there are those who cultivate precepts and meditative concentration, and who are able to give rise to a heart of true faith toward these profound passages concerning cause and effect.
There are two reasons for being able to believe: first, it clarifies that one has served many Buddhas over successive lifetimes to manifest the causes of faith; that is to say, this is not...
This person is no ordinary individual. How could they have planted roots of goodness under only one or two Buddhas?
Rather, they have resolved upon bodhicitta in the presence of immeasurable thousands of millions of Buddhas, planting various roots of goodness such as non-attachment.

Now, if those who give rise to pure faith for even a single thought-moment possess such vast, profound, and firm roots of goodness, how much more so those who have attained permanent, non-retrogressive faith!
Second, the explanation of the Buddhas’ reception and the accomplishment of the virtue of faith, which also has two parts.
First, the explanation of the Buddhas’ reception as a gateway to manifesting merit and virtue: [The Buddha] addressed Subhūti, saying, "The Tathāgata, with all..."
This is known through direct perception and seen with the Buddha-eye. These sentient beings of pure faith obtain such immeasurable merit within their activities of walking, standing, and acting.
The two characters "such" (如是) refer back to the aforementioned vast and inexhaustible roots of goodness.
Why is this? These sentient beings no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a being, or the notion of a life-span.

They have no notion of dharmas, nor do they have any notion of non-dharmas. Why is this? If these sentient beings were to grasp at signs with their minds, they would be attached to a self, a person, a being, and a life-span.
If they were to grasp at the sign of dharmas, they would likewise be attached to a self, a person, a being, and a life-span. Why?
For this reason, if one grasps at the signs of what is not the Dharma, one becomes attached to the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Second, the explanation of the reason for "receiving and upholding" reveals the gate of wisdom. First, it poses a general inquiry:
"Now, pure faith in a single thought-moment is rare; by what principle do all Buddhas know and see it? The intent of the explanation is as follows: [There is none.]
Those with pure faith stubbornly cling to the five aggregates within their body and mind as a sovereign master; this is called the mark of self (*ātman*).

Because they calculate a self, they give rise to delusions and create karma, transmigrating through various realms of existence; these are called *pudgala*, which translates as "one who repeatedly takes up [existence]," and are termed the mark of person (*pudgala-nimitta*).
They calculate the fluctuations of the self—its prosperity and decline, its suffering and pleasure—and perceive it as arising in a continuous succession.

The characteristic of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*) refers to the reckoning of a single life-continuum (*jīvitendriya*). The characteristic of a life-span (*āyuṣka-nimitta*) refers to the three factors of consciousness, warmth, and breath remaining connected and uninterrupted.
These four are collectively the characteristic of a self (*ātma-nimitta*). Now, one who possesses pure faith does not cling to these four characteristics within the five aggregates of body and mind;
thus, the self is empty. Furthermore, they do not give rise to [clinging] toward the five aggregates of body and mind.
When the conceptualization of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is [realized as] empty of phenomena, one does not dwell even in that emptiness of phenomena;

hence it is said that there is also no mark of non-phenomena (*adharma-lakṣaṇa*). Because true emptiness is uninterrupted, even non-phenomena do not exist. Thus, by departing from these two attachments, one accomplishes pure faith.
To be sustained by the knowledge and vision of all Buddhas is the very root for attaining merit. Next, the section beginning with "For what reason" (*kasmāt*) reiterates the three preceding meanings.
First, it poses a question: "How is it known that those with pure faith sever the two attachments to self and phenomena?"

The meaning of this explanation is as follows: Now, regarding pure faith, if there is attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*) and the mind grasps at various signs (*nimitta*), one then clings to the four marks such as "self" and so forth.

Since one does not grasp at signs, it is known that there is no attachment to a self. If there is attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) and the mind grasps at the signs of phenomena, one likewise clings to the four marks such as "self.
This is because phenomena are the root and the self is the sprout; where there is a root, there must necessarily be...

There are sprouts. Where there is attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), there must necessarily be attachment to a self (*ātman-grāha*). Since there is no [attachment to] a self, one knows that there is no attachment to phenomena.
Later, he further inquires: "Attachment to phenomena is merely the characteristic of phenomena; for what reason does one then become attached to a self? The meaning of the explanation is as follows:
If grasping at what is not the Dharma (adharma) also constitutes attachment to a self, how much more so is this true for grasping at the Dharma? This latter statement explains the former.

Thus we know that even the slightest grasping or attachment falls into the dust of dharmas (dharmarajas) and possesses the four marks of a self (ātman). Therefore, those with pure faith should especially ensure that both the Dharma and non-Dharma are completely exhausted.
Therefore, one should not grasp at the Dharma, nor should one grasp at what is not the Dharma. For this reason, the Tathāgata has constantly said:
"O bhikṣus, you should understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the simile of a raft. Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."
Therefore, because one previously grasped both the Dharma and non-Dharma due to attachment to a self, this admonition that one "should not" [grasp them] leads directly into the Middle Way.
That is to say, one should not grasp the Dharma and become attached to existence, nor should one grasp non-Dharma and become attached to emptiness.
Because of this principle of non-attachment, the Tathāgata has constantly said: "You bhikṣus..."
One must understand that all the teachings I have spoken are merely provisional words used to manifest the meaning.

A student must grasp the meaning and forget the words, just as in the analogy of abandoning the raft after crossing the river. The raft is the means for crossing the river; once the shore is reached, it is abandoned.

The Tathāgata has preached that dharmas are non-dharmas; they are merely rafts for crossing over the Dharma. Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone non-Dharma—how could one not relinquish it?
To still cling to the raft after having already crossed the river—how is this different from one who has not yet crossed the river?
If one has already abandoned the Dharma yet still dwells in non-Dharma, there is no difference between such a person and one who has not abandoned the Dharma at all.
By not dwelling in the Dharma, one does not fall into existence; by not dwelling in non-Dharma, one does not fall into emptiness.
Entering the profound gate of the Middle Way, one is then able to accord with the cause of non-dwelling and the fruit of signlessness. This is called "purity in accordance with reality."
This is the section on Faith.
The third doubt states: It was previously taught that one cannot see the Buddha through signs, for the Buddha is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Thus, it would seem inappropriate for there to be anything attained or anything spoken. Why, then, does the Tathāgata attain *bodhi* and preach the Dharma?
“Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
Or has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma? Subhūti replied, “World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught...”
There is no fixed dharma that is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can speak.
Why is this? All dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and ineffable; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
Why is this so? It is because all worthy ones and sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma.
Regarding this severance of the signless, how can doubt be spoken of? There are two sections: first, the resolution of doubt through question and answer;
second, the comparative evaluation that reveals its excellence. Now, for the first, the resolution of doubt. The Buddha asked:
"In your mind, do you think that the Tathāgata attained *bodhi* beneath the Bodhi tree? Or do you think that the Tathāgata [attained it] during the various assemblies in the past or future?"
"Is it the Dharma that has been taught? Śūnyatā-saṃbhava immediately grasped his meaning and replied: "The people of the world all say that the Tathāgata has something attained and something taught.
However, when the Tathāgata understands the meaning of what the Buddha taught, it is not so.
This is because there must necessarily be a dharma called 'bodhi' for one to attain it; yet now, since there is no fixed or substantial dharma, what is there to be attained? It can be seen thus."
The manifestation beneath the Bodhi tree was a transformation according to the capacities of beings; it was not the Dharmakāya Buddha in its true sense.
Only when there is a fixed dharma can one speak of it. Now, since there is no fixed or substantial dharma, what is there to be spoken?

One can see that all the various assemblies before and after were expedient means according to capacity, devoid of any real dharma. This has been explained consistently from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Answer: Therefore, the verse of Maitreya states: "The manifested transformation is not the true Buddha, nor is it the speaker of the Dharma.

The teaching of the Dharma is non-dual and without grasping; there is no speaking, as it is free from the characteristics of words. The meaning is that while conventional existence is real, ultimate existence is non-existent.

The characteristics of the manifested transformation exist based upon the conventional; however, because the answer relies upon the ultimate truth, it says that there is no fixed dharma. Thus it is said: "Beginning from the attainment..."
From the night [of the Enlightenment] until his final Parinirvāṇa, throughout this interval, he never spoke a single word.
Why is this? The meaning of the inquiry is: why is there no fixed dharma that can be spoken? The meaning of the explanation is:
the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is none other than the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); because it is free from the marks of mental objects, it cannot be grasped, and it transcends words.
Because it is characterized by such [inexpressible] marks, it cannot be spoken of. Because it lacks the mark of existence, it is called "not a dharma.
Because it lacks the mark of non-existence, it is called "not a non-dharma. This is what is meant: "The one who preaches the Dharma has neither speech nor demonstration;
the one who listens to the Dharma has neither hearing nor attainment. Why is this so? The intent of the inquiry is to say that this state of neither attainment nor speech is the absence of...

Regarding "unconditioned dharmas" (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*): this is the principle of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). It is fundamentally devoid of names and characteristics and does not involve speech or thought;

how, then, could there be distinctions among the worthies and sages of the three vehicles? The intent of this explanation is that the distinctions among the worthies and sages of the three vehicles all exist within the undifferentiated dharma of the unconditioned, just like the analogy of the three animals crossing a river. The river— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "The river," indicating the source material was incomplete.*
There is no shallowness or depth in [the Dharma itself]; rather, shallowness and depth reside in the sentient beings. The unconditioned dharmas (asaṃskṛta-dharma) have no differentiation;
however, differentiation exists in the wisdom capable of realizing them through the three vehicles (triyāna). It is merely that there are differences of great and small, shallow and deep.
Second, the comparison that reveals superiority. Above, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma was explained as being beyond verbal appropriation;

this was done for fear that people might wish to utterly discard and abolish the verbal teachings. How could they know that although the Dharma cannot be grasped or expressed in words, one may nevertheless enter it by means of speech?
Thus, the comparison is made to reveal its superiority, so that people will receive, uphold, and propagate it.
[The Buddha] said: "Subhūti, what do you think?

If someone were to fill the great trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti replied: "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Why is this? Because that merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if there is someone who receives, upholds, and even recites as little as a four-line verse from this sutra and explains it to others, their merit will surpass that [previous merit]. Why is this? Subhūti, because all Buddhas and the unsurpassed...
The Dharma of *samyaksambodhi* all issues from this sutra. Subhūti, that which is called the Buddha-dharma is itself not the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha first raised the question of worldly merit, saying: suppose there were someone who filled a great trichiliocosm with the seven treasures...
"If one were to give as a gift [this many], would the merit obtained not be great? Regarding the "trichiliocosm" (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*), the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states:
"A thousand sets of four continents, suns and moons, Mount Sumeru, the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the Brahma worlds, is called a 'small chiliocosm' (*sāhasracūḍikā lokadhātu*).

A thousand times this small chiliocosm is called a 'medium chiliocosm' (*dvisāhasro madhyamo lokadhātuḥ*). A thousand times this medium chiliocosm is a 'great trichiliocosm' (*trisāhasramahāsāhasraḥ*). All these undergo formation and destruction simultaneously. — Thus it was spoken by Ākāśaghoṣa.
The meaning is this: the seven treasures are most precious, and the trichiliocosm is likewise most vast. Yet, by offering even seven coins to the Buddha, one obtains immeasurable merit;
how much more so for many treasures? Therefore, it is said that they are "very many. Furthermore, he raises a self-reflexive inquiry: "Why is it said that they are many?"
This is not discussed in terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) regarding the nature of that merit; rather, it is spoken of in terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Since it is indeed spoken of according to conventional truth, worldly merit is specifically not as superior as the supramundane merit of upholding this sutra.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "Furthermore, if there should be someone who, within this sutra, [regards] non-self as previously described..."
This is for the sake of delivering sentient beings. It is the practice of giving without dwelling upon signs. A Buddha cannot be seen through signs;
the Dharma cannot be expressed in words. One should receive it with a single thought of pure faith and a sincere mind, reverently upholding it—either in its entirety.
Or if one were to uphold even as little as a four-line verse, and furthermore explain its meaning and intent to others, the merit obtained would be even more superior than that.
One might ask: why does upholding a four-line verse from the sutra suddenly surpass the merit of giving away the treasures of a great trichiliocosm?
The intention is that although such giving of treasures is vast, it is merely worldly, conditioned merit; in the end...

One cannot attain unsurpassed bodhi. As for even a single four-line verse of this sutra, it is from this that the reward-body (*sambhogakāya*) and transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of all Buddhas, as well as the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas, are born;
there is nothing that does not arise from it. Why is this? Although the dharma-body is neither born nor extinguished, it remains hidden when shrouded by afflictions. Wisdom...
When wisdom realizes it, [the Dharma-body] becomes manifest. This sutra exclusively elucidates wondrous wisdom; does it not serve as the cause of realization for the Dharma-body?
The two bodies of retribution and transformation are brought about by myriad practices. This sutra guides wondrous practice through wondrous wisdom;

does it not serve as the cause of birth for the bodies of retribution and transformation? Its merit is such that it alone surpasses the blessings derived from bestowing jewels throughout the great trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, what is called "the Buddha-dharma emerging from this sutra" exists only in terms of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If one seeks the characteristics of delusion and enlightenment, or of sage and ordinary person, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are utterly unfindable;
thus, it is not the case that the so-called Buddha-dharma emerges from this sutra. Therefore, the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuanjue jing*) says: "All Tathāgatas' Perfect Enlightenment..."
O Wondrous Mind! Originally there is neither bodhi nor nirvana; there is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the failure to attain it.

Beginning with the non-attainment of bodhi and concluding with that which is not even the Buddha-dharma, the beginning and end correspond to one another, and thus the purport of the sutra becomes ever more clear.

The fourth doubt states: Since the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) of the sages cannot be grasped or explained, why is it that the śrāvakas each realize their respective fruits and speak according to what they have realized? This is divided into four sections regarding the four fruits.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a srotāpanna (stream-enterer) have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A srotāpanna is called one who has entered the stream, yet there is nothing entered.
He does not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; therefore he is called a srotāpanna."
This refers to the doubt regarding the attainment of the fruits by Śrāvakas through abandonment. First, the initial fruit is raised for questioning: Srotāpanna.

This is translated as "Entering the Stream. One has already abandoned the eighty-eight latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) of the delusions of view, including greed, anger, ignorance, and pride within the three realms.
He has entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*). It is said that he does not form such a thought as, "Have I attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*?
Śūnyatā-jīvita replied: "He does not form such a thought. Why is this? Because that *srotāpanna* has already severed the coarse afflictions of discrimination within the three realms;
thus he is called one who has entered the stream of the noble ones. In reality, however, there is not a single dharma [that exists] as..."
That which constitutes "entry" is simply the non-appropriation of the six sensory objects—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—and this is what is called being a *srotāpanna*.
How could there be some separate dharma that serves as the object of entry? It is precisely through non-appropriation that one attains the fruit;
why then do you doubt that there is appropriation? If one still harbors the discriminative thought, "I am able to attain the fruit," that itself constitutes attachment.
"I am but an ordinary person. How could I be called one who has entered the stream of the noble ones and attained the first fruit?
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a Sakṛdāgāmin have the thought: 'I have attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A Sakṛdāgāmin is so named because he returns only once more. And...
In reality, there is no coming or going; this is called a Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner).

Next, he asks about the second fruit: the Sakṛdāgāmin—here translated as "One who returns once more"—has already severed the first six of the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
With three grades of residual afflictions yet remaining, they must return once more to the desire realm to undergo [rebirth].
Śāriputra asked, "Does he have such a thought as, 'I have attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin'? Śūnyatājanman replied, "He does not have such a thought. Why is this?
That Sakṛdāgāmin is called 'one who comes and goes once,' yet in reality there is no coming or going.
This is because he has already realized the emptiness of the self; who is it that comes and goes? If one still perceives coming and going, one is merely following after delusion."
If one who has attained this has not yet eliminated the mark of self (*ātman*), how can they be called one who has attained the second fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*)?
Viewed from this perspective, the *srotāpanna* does not even grasp at their own fruit.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Anāgāmin have the thought, ‘I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin’?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One. Why is this? An Anāgāmin is called ‘one who does not return,’ yet in reality there is no such thing as ‘not returning. For this reason, he is named Anāgāmin.”

Furthermore, he questioned him by citing the three fruits of the path. Regarding the *anāgāmin*—which is translated here as "one who does not return"—it refers to one whose nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) pertaining to the realm of desire have been exhausted, such that they will no longer return to the realm of desire to undergo rebirth.
Subhūti replied: "He does not form such a thought. Why is this? Because:
The Anāgāmin extinguishes the nine grades of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the desire realm simultaneously; having no further dwelling below, they are called "Non-returners" (*Anāgāmin*).
Yet, in reality, there is no such thing as "not returning. This is because they have already realized non-self (*anātman*): who is it that does not return?
If one still perceives a person who "does not return," then the mark of self (*ātman*) still persists; how, then, can they be named "Non-returners"?
Viewed in this light, even the Anāgāmin does not grasp at his own fruit.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Arhat have the thought, "I have attained the path of Arhatship"?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Truly, there is no dharma that is called 'Arhat'."
“World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to think, ‘I have attained the path of Arhatship,’ he would immediately be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
World-Honored One, the Buddha has said that I am foremost among men in the attainment of the Samādhi of Non-contention.”

"I am an Arhat who has attained freedom from desire. World-Honored One, if I were to have such a thought—that "I have attained the path of Arhatship"—then the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇā (non-contention).
This is because, in reality, Subhūti has no practice at all; it is for this reason that he is named Subhūti.
This refers to delighting in the practice of araṇya (forest dwelling).
Later, he questioned him regarding the four fruits [of the spiritual path]. "Arhat" here is translated as "one who is no longer subject to rebirth" (*anuppāda*).

This is because his afflictions (*kleśa*) within the three realms have been exhausted, and he will not undergo further existence. That is to say, he had this thought: "Have I attained the path of Arhatship?"

Yes. Śūnyatā-utpanna replied, "He does not form such a thought. Why is this? An Arhat is simply one for whom the afflictions of view and thought within the triple world have been purified and exhausted, and who has realized the true suchness of selflessness. In reality, there is no dharma that can be called 'Arhat.
If he were to lower his mind and form the thought, 'I have attained the path of an Arhat,' then he would [be a person with a conceit of attainment]."
If one clings to the four marks such as "self" and so forth, one is no different from an ordinary person; how, then, can one be called an Arhat?
Furthermore, he cites his own case by way of analogy, saying: "The Buddha previously stated that Subhūti has attained the Samādhi of Non-contention (araṇā-samādhi).
As for this Samādhi of Non-contention, because there is no self, one does not vex others. If one dislikes sitting, one stands; one does not compete with others."
I am neither right nor wrong; this causes others not to give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*). This practice is supreme; therefore, it is said that he is the foremost among men.
Kumārajīva stated: "There are two kinds of non-contention (*araṇā*): first, by the power of samādhi, one protects sentient beings so that they do not give rise to a contentious mind;
second, by conforming to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one is without conflict or contention. All arhats [possess this].
One who is free from the afflictions of craving for the three realms is called an Arhat free from desire.
Because I am without contention, I am designated as the foremost among all Arhats free from desire. Although I have received such a seal of approval from the Buddha, [I remain humble].
Yet I do not form such a thought as: "I am an Arhat free from desire. If one were to form such a thought, there would be a self.

All disputes arise from the existence of a self. The World-Honored One would then not say of Subhūti that he is one who delights in the practice of araṇā. *Araṇā* here means "tranquility," which is to say, "non-dispute. Dispute—
This is because they are noisy and bustling; it is said that they are not people who delight in practicing the conduct of tranquility.
Since Subhūti has, in reality, no practice whatsoever, he is named "Subhūti, one who delights in the practice of araṇā.
If this is so for Subhūti, then why should there be any doubt regarding the śrāvakas who have attained the fruits and are without grasping?
The fifth doubt states: Śākyamuni, during his causal stage as the Seer Suprabuddha, received a prophecy from the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara;
yet Dīpaṃkara preached the Dharma to Śākyamuni. How can it be said that "the teaching is not to be grasped"?
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think? Did the Tathāgata, when he was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma?
No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly obtained no dharma."

This is the refutation of the doubt regarding Śākyamuni’s reception of the prediction from Dīpaṃkara. Fearing that there might be doubt regarding the attainment of something, he therefore questioned Subhūti:
"When the Tathāgata was formerly at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha and received his prediction, did he obtain anything in terms of dharmas?
Subhūti answered directly: "There was nothing obtained. Why? Because the "reception of a prediction" is merely words; it is not...
This is realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*). If so, by what means is one granted a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*)?

To be granted a prediction is simply to realize the principle of non-differentiation within one's own non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*). It is merely that wisdom merges with the principle and the object merges with the spirit;
how could there be anything said or anything attained?
