[The record] concludes. His lifespan was increased by ten years. He returned to exhort the people of the world to recite [the scriptures], and his soul was restored from the netherworld.

He submitted a detailed report, and an imperial envoy was dispatched to Hao to inspect the stele; it was indeed as described. Examining the two treatises, both contained commentaries; they were subsequently added to the canon for circulation.

The nineteenth doubt arises from the thirteenth section of the third chapter.

Since the text therein states that no dharma is attained in the realization of bodhi, the treatise asks: "If the Tathāgata does not attain a single dharma, how can the Tathāgata, through the successive stages of superior realization, progressively attain bodhi?"

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, when the Buddha attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is it that there is nothing to be attained? The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is, Subhūti.
Regarding my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be attained; this is called *anuttara-samyak-”
The three types of enlightenment. Furthermore, Subhūti, this Dharma is equal; it has no high or low. This is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

By practicing all wholesome dharmas without a self, without a person, without a sentient being, and without a life-span, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti, as for what is called "wholesome" [dharmas]...
As for "Dharma," the Tathāgata says it is not a dharma; it is called a "good dharma. This raises the doubt:
how can one practice and realize that which is the cessation of all dharmas? Subhūti asks:
regarding Bodhi, does the Buddha have something to attain, or has he nothing to attain? The answer consists of three sections. First: taking the non-attainment of any dharma as perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha first confirmed his words, saying: "So it is, so it is. Regarding my awakening (*bodhi*), there is not the slightest dharma that can be attained;

this is called 'attaining awakening. Second, one takes equality as perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). That which has neither high nor low means: because it does not increase when among the noble ones (*ārya*), it is without high;
because it does not diminish when abiding among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it is without low. As the verse says: 'The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) does not increase.'"

Third, through the cultivation of goodness by means of the primary and auxiliary practices, one achieves perfect enlightenment. This means that although [the nature of reality] is equal, one does not achieve perfect enlightenment without cultivation.
One must cultivate various wholesome dharmas, such as non-self and so forth, and only then will one achieve it.

Non-self and so forth are the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*), which is the direct path (*mārga*). Cultivating all wholesome dharmas is the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*), which is the auxiliary path (*upāya-mārga*).

Furthermore, "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" is perfect enlightenment. As for what is called "wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas characterized by attachment and outflows;
rather, they are wholesome dharmas that are free from characteristics and without outflows. Question: Third.
Regarding the twelfth, the thirteenth, and this intervening section—these four locations all state that one cannot attain *bodhi*. How are they to be distinguished? Answer:
Although the preceding and following texts are similar in form, their underlying meanings differ. The third [section] raises doubt regarding Śākyamuni’s attainment of the fruit;
the twelfth raises doubt regarding the causes for Sudhana’s attainment of *bodhi*; and the thirteenth raises doubt regarding the absence [of such causes].
The Dharma has no Buddha. These nineteen doubts involve both cultivation and realization; their four meanings are distinct and clearly delineated, without any confusion.
○ The twentieth doubt states: "If one attains Bodhi by cultivating wholesome dharmas, why did you previously repeatedly state that upholding and expounding [the sutra] can accomplish Bodhi?
Furthermore, the dharmas that are spoken do not depart from names, phrases, and phonemes. These three—"
All are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Since dharmas that are indeterminate possess neither cause nor effect, how could they constitute bodhi?

Subhūti, if someone were to take all the Sumeru kings and such heaps of the seven treasures as exist within a trichiliocosm and offer them as a gift, yet another person were to take this *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*—
Even if one were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even as little as a four-line stanza from this sutra, the previously mentioned merit would not equal a hundredth part of it;
it would not equal a thousand-million-billionth part, nor could it be reached by any calculation, number, or analogy.

This refutation addresses the doubt that what is described as "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) cannot be the cause [of awakening]. That is to say, although it is said to be indeterminate, it is in fact the direct cause of Bodhi.
For the Sūtras expound the True Principle; by means of them one attains realization, and based on that realization one initiates practice, thereby finally attaining Bodhi.
If there were no gateway of the teachings, how could one know where to enter? Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "By the gateway of the Buddha's teaching, one emerges..."
Because the three realms are suffering, even the offering of Mount Sumeru as a precious gift does not equal the merit of a single verse. A verse by Maitreya says:
"Although it is called an indeterminate dharma, it is taught to be the cause of that [enlightenment]. Therefore, a single jewel of the Dharma surpasses immeasurable worldly treasures.
That [jewel] is precisely bodhi. Question: How does this differ from the ninth doubt? Answer: The former concerns the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

The objection regarding "lack of essence" (asvabhāva) is an objection based on [the fact that] the indeterminate (avyākṛta) is not a cause. Furthermore, that [objection] is based solely on the difficulty concerning "retention" (dhāraṇa), whereas this [objection] additionally addresses wholesome phenomena (kuśala-dharma); thus, they are fundamentally different.
The twenty-first doubt states: "If it is said that this Dharma is equal, with no high or low, how is it that the Tathāgata delivers sentient beings?
Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has such a thought as, 'I shall deliver sentient beings.'"
“Subhūti, do not conceive such a thought. Why is that? In reality, there are no sentient beings who have been delivered by the Tathāgata.
If there were any sentient beings delivered by the Tathāgata, then the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata speaks of a ‘self,’ it is not a self at all; yet ordinary people imagine that there is a self.”
Subhūti, those who are called "ordinary beings" by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, ordinary beings; they are merely designated as "ordinary beings.
This is the severance of equality; how does it resolve doubts regarding birth? First, to prevent erroneous understanding, it says: "Do not say that the Tathāgata delivers sentient beings;
do not entertain such a thought under any circumstances. Second, to demonstrate the correct view, it asks: "By what meaning..."
Therefore, it is said that in reality there are no sentient beings who attain *nirvāṇa*. This is because within the equal and true *dharmadhātu*, the Buddha does not deliver sentient beings;
for the conventional designation "sentient being" shares its basis with the aggregates (*skandhas*) and is not separate from the *dharmadhātu*. As the treatise states:

"The provisional name 'sentient being' and the real dharmas of the five aggregates are both not separate from the *dharmadhātu*. Thus, there are no sentient beings who attain *nirvāṇa*. (3) The Refutation.

To explain why this is so: if the Tathāgata possessed such a mind as to think that there are sentient beings within the five aggregates who can be saved, then there would be the marks of a self, a person, and so forth.
Furthermore, to successively sweep away these traces, it is said: although the Buddha speaks of a "self," fundamentally there is no self;

those who cling to a self are merely ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Yet, even though one speaks of an "ordinary worldling," there is likewise no such thing as an ordinary worldling. This is, for example, like...
In a dream one sees a tiger; yet both the tiger and the person in the dream are ungraspable. Nevertheless, because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cling to a self, it is said that "it is not the self.

Fearing that they might cling to [the notion of] being ordinary beings, it is said that "it is not an ordinary being. Thus, by gradually eliminating clinging thoughts, it is said that "traces are successively brushed away.
However, although the texts in all four preceding sections are identical in stating that there is no one to deliver sentient beings, yet...

The intention differs. Initially, one seeks to liberate sentient beings by detaching from the notion of a self; yet, the eleventh doubt is that the one capable of liberating others must be a self, and the fourteenth doubt is that if there is no self, who is it that liberates?
These twenty-one doubts [arise] regarding the equality of the true realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is incompatible with the liberation of sentient beings.
The similarities and differences are clear; they must be carefully distinguished.
○ The twenty-second doubt arises from the seventeenth. According to what was previously stated: "It is not a body endowed with form;

"Endowed. The meaning is this: the Dharma-body is ultimately without marks or characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), yet these marks and characteristics have never ceased to be the Buddha.

If one does not investigate the root of the Dharmakāya but merely compares and observes the Tathāgata through the derivative thirty-two marks—given that the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks manifest based upon the Dharmakāya—the [comparison with a] Wheel-Turning King...

The King was born according to the causes of his karma; as for the vast difference between the ordinary and the sage, how can one find a standard of comparison? When the four emptinesses arise, one immediately realizes that the Buddha is not to be seen through forms.

Seeking through sounds and voices, one merely sees what is seen and hears what is heard; this is the biased and heterodox path of ordinary beings and those of limited capacity, unable to perceive the Perfectly Enlightened Tathāgata.
Why is this? The Dharma-body is not an object of consciousness; it is free from all marks and is the realm of true wisdom, known only through direct realization.

Regarding the Buddhas of the Dharma-body: the Dharma-body is invisible and cannot be known by that [ordinary] consciousness.

The signless and unconditioned are the causes for cultivating merit; however, these only produce results characterized by signs. Since results characterized by signs are not the fruit of Buddhahood, it follows that the fruit of Buddhahood has no connection with meritorious signs.

This refutes the doubt that the Buddha-fruit is unrelated to the marks of merit. The text has four parts. First, it prohibits thoughts that disparage the marks.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The form-body is not the Buddha; the voice is likewise so. Yet, without departing from form and voice, one perceives the Buddha’s supernormal powers.

Third, it clarifies that the marks of merit are not lost: these are the marks of fulfillment, which are precisely the marks of merit.
These are the causes—the five perfections (*pāramitā*)—cultivated in the Mahāyāna, and the fruits of the merit thereby obtained. One need only remain free from the marks of grasping and attachment.
This differs from the Hinayana view of annihilationism; therefore, it is said that regarding phenomena, one does not speak of the characteristic of annihilation. The *Śāstra* states:
"In this context, in order to negate the notion of absolute quiescence, it is shown that there is no abiding in nirvana. Fourth, the reason for non-loss is explained in two parts.

First, it is explained that because one has attained *kṣānti*, there is no loss. *Kṣānti* refers here to the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena), which is attained at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The bodhisattva’s realization attains the merit of the patience of non-self (*anātman-kṣānti*), which surpasses the merit of giving away treasures as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Wuzhuo says: "This demonstrates not being attached to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). If one dwells in birth-and-death, one then receives [the karmic] blessings. Furthermore, he poses a question and provides an explanation: "Why is this?"
One does not accept merit because there is no greedy attachment. Greedy attachment constitutes a cause for the outflows (*āsrava*);

even if one were to obtain the thirty-two marks, one would merely be equal to a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). If one does not give rise to greedy attachment, then the cause becomes free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
The thirty-two marks thus obtained adorn the Dharma-body; this is what is called a Buddha.
The twenty-fourth doubt: [The questioner] has come from above with the premise that bodhisattvas do not accept merit.
If bodhisattvas do not accept merit, how is it that the merit of the Buddhas is received and utilized by sentient beings? According to the lifespan of a Buddha, it should be a full hundred years;
yet, upon reaching eighty, he enters nirvana, intentionally leaving behind twenty years of merit for future generations.
The disciples enjoy it. Furthermore, if one makes offerings and serves the Buddha, one can obtain immeasurable merit;
this too is the Buddha’s merit, which sentient beings are able to enjoy.
Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore he is called the Tathāgata.
This addresses the doubt regarding the appearance of the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and the reception of merit. The text has two parts. First, the refutation of erroneous interpretations:
it states that if anyone says the Tathāgata appears, comes, enters parinirvāṇa, or departs, they do not understand the meaning of what the Buddha taught.
Second, the presentation of the correct view: it says that he "comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. The verse says: "Going..."

The manifested transformation Buddha comes; the Tathāgata is eternally immovable. As for the "great clouds," it is said that when the water of the sentient beings' minds is pure, they perceive the Buddha coming.
He comes from nowhere. When they see the Twin Trees and perceive his extinction, they say the Buddha has departed.
Yet he departs to no destination. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any nirvāṇa. It is merely...
By the power of skillful means, he manifests the dharma of sovereign mastery. If this is so, since there is not even a Buddha who appears, how could there be the matter of receiving blessings?
It is merely that the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) responds to the capacities of sentient beings, appearing to have emergence and disappearance.

The twenty-fifth doubt: Based on the preceding point that a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) cannot be used as a standard to infer the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it appears that the Dharma-body—which is without coming, going, sitting, or reclining—is distinct from the transformation body.
Yet, based on the negation of the notion of annihilation and the manifestation of the non-loss of meritorious marks, it appears that the Dharma-body and the transformation body are one.
Thus, this doubt arises. The Buddha addresses this by means of worlds as numerous as motes of dust.
He provides an extensive explanation of the meaning of neither identity nor difference in order to sever this doubt:
"Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to grind the trichiliocosm into fine dust, what do you think?
Would that mass of atoms be numerous? "It would be very numerous, World-Honored One. Why is that?"
If this multitude of atoms were truly existent, the Buddha would not have called it a "multitude of atoms.
Why is that? The Buddha said: "A multitude of atoms is not a multitude of atoms; it is merely named a 'multitude of atoms.
World-Honored One, the so-called "trichiliocosm" spoken of by the Tathāgata is not a world; it is merely named a "world. For what reason? If the world...
If the elements were substantially existent, they would be a "unified whole. The Tathāgata has said that what is a unified whole is not a unified whole;
it is merely called a "unified whole. Subhūti, that which is a unified whole is inexpressible;
yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things.

This concerns the doubt regarding whether the Dharma-body and the Transformation-body are identical or distinct. The text has two parts: first, refuting identity and difference by means of the world and its atoms;

second, refuting the self and dharmas by means of śamatha and vipaśyanā. This is the first part. It further has three sections. First, it indicates the identity and difference of the world and its atoms to reveal their lack of intrinsic nature.
Regarding the term "world," it is a metaphor for the Dharma-body. Regarding "atoms," they are a metaphor for the Response-body (Nirmāṇakāya). [The text continues: "To shatter the world..."

They constitute the objects; yet objects have no distinct nature. When objects combine, they form the realms; yet the realms have no singular nature. This serves as an analogy for the arising of the total phenomena (dharmas); yet the total response has no distinct nature.
The total response is itself the phenomena; yet the phenomena have no singular nature. Nevertheless, the essence and function of the Tathāgata are mutually interfused.
Thus, it is that which is able to be both one and different, neither one nor different, sovereign and unimpeded.

This is an explanation based on Vasubandhu’s *Commentary on the Diamond Sutra* (*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) for the purpose of severing doubts; whereas Asaṅga’s explanation, for the purpose of destroying attachments, states: "In order to destroy the body of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-kāya*)."
Therefore, it is said that the elements, sense objects, and so forth [are analyzed]. Within this, there are two kinds of skillful means:

first, the skillful means of pulverization; second, the skillful means of non-perception. "Non-perception" refers to non-recollection. When Ākāśagena replied that they were "very many," this was the skillful means of pulverization used to break down gross form.
Second, the explanation of the analogy of the subtle atom (paramāṇu) shows that the response body (nirmāṇakāya) has no difference from its nature. By...
For what reason is it called an "atom" (*paramāṇu*)? It is because it lacks substantial reality. Furthermore, it is asked:
"Why is it called an 'empty atom' and yet also called an 'atom'? The intent of the explanation is as follows: That which the Buddha speaks of is not a real atom, but an "empty atom.
Because an atom is ground into powder, it is not a single entity; because many atoms aggregate together, they are called "atoms."
Therefore, they are not different. Thus, the verse says: "In this realm of the Dharma, there is neither oneness nor difference. Wuzhuo says:
"This refers to the expedient of non-recollection used to shatter the subtle dust [of conceptualization]. Third, the explanation of the analogy of the world: the Dharmakāya has no single nature.
This means that it is not only the subtle dust that is produced which is empty, but furthermore, the world that produces it is also empty. There is none.
The commentary states: "This uses the skillful means of non-recollection to dismantle the world. This 'dismantling' refers to the body, which is the sentient world.
Because mental phenomena have no substance and cannot be analyzed, they are dismantled solely through the skillful means of non-recollection."
This means that when one is mindful of it, it exists; when one is not mindful, it does not exist. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "When the mind arises, phenomena arise;

when the mind ceases, phenomena cease. Furthermore, both [the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith*] employ the analysis of elemental particles (*dhātu*) to refute the notion of a composite whole.

The text poses the question: "Why do you say the world is empty? It explains: "If the world were truly existent, it would be a single, indistinguishable unity of all its constituent particles, and could not be divided."
This is the characteristic of their conjunction. Thus, there should not be many; yet now the Tathāgata speaks of three thousand, clarifying that they are not a single, indistinct unity.
This is the refutation of the "one realm" by means of the "three thousand. Regarding the phrase "the conjunction of one is not a conjunction," the intent of the explanation is as follows:
when the Buddha speaks of the conjunction of one, it is not a truly existent conjunction; rather, it is a conjunction of emptiness and non-existence. This...

A "unified whole" has no essence that can be described; it is merely for the sake of ordinary people who, giving rise to false attachment and being deluded regarding phenomenal dharmas, give rise to afflictions.
Subhūti, if someone were to say, "The Buddha has taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span," what do you think, Subhūti?
Would that person understand the meaning of what I have taught? "No, World-Honored One, that person would not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught.
Why is this? Because the World-Honored One has said that the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span..."

To see thus is not to have a view of self, a view of a person, a view of a sentient being, or a view of a life-span. These are what are called the view of self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.

Subhūti, those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all phenomena, know them thus, see them thus, and believe and understand them thus, so that they do not give rise to the notion of phenomena.
Subhūti, that which is called the "characteristic of phenomena" (dharmalakṣaṇa) is, according to the Tathāgata, not a characteristic of phenomena;
it is merely designated as the "characteristic of phenomena. This refers to the destruction of the self and phenomena through śamatha and vipaśyanā.

To destroy the views of self and phenomena, one must necessarily attain fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna), for only then are the views of self and phenomena eliminated. To attain this fundamental wisdom, one must first cultivate preparatory wisdom (prayoga-jñāna).

Through skillful means—such as tranquility and insight, concentration and wisdom, and meditative equipoise—one contemplates the two kinds of selflessness (of persons and phenomena) and does not give rise to conceptual discrimination.

Upon reaching the direct realization of *tathatā* (suchness), this constitutes the attainment of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Forgetting conditions and entering into principle is the essential gateway of this practice.
First, one must shatter the grasping at a self; for if it were said that the Buddha taught views of a self and so forth as being truly existent, [it would be a grave error].
This person does not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. Why do they not understand?
They think that when the Buddha speaks of views such as "self" and "person," these are not real views of self and person; rather, they are merely provisional designations for self and person.

Sentient beings fail to understand this and take them to be real. It is like a fly perceiving a snake—how could that be a real perception? Next, the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is refuted, as follows:
Not only is the view of a self non-existent, but the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) are likewise empty.
Those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta should further contemplate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Therefore, within the midst of daily life, regarding all phenomena, one should employ the superior mind (*adhimukti-citta*) and superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) as skillful means (*upāya*). What are "all phenomena"? Within the ten dharma realms, whether they be noble or...

In general, whether it be the basis or the object—ranging from the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of sentient beings below, up to the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*) of the Buddhas above—one relies upon *śamatha* to stifle all external conditions until only the mind remains;

thus, with a clarity that is never obscured, one knows that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self (*anātman*). Relying thus upon *vipaśyanā*, one observes everything and investigates it in meticulous detail.

Seeking [this], one sees it with vivid clarity. Seeing that all marks are non-marks, one thus relies upon *dhyāna*, maintaining the equilibrium of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*), becoming unimpeded and sovereign.
Although one has not yet personally realized *tathatā* (suchness), this already constitutes a proximate expedient for the fundamental non-conceptual correct gnosis.
Internally transforming *tathatā* into an object of faith and understanding, one’s faith becomes pure; thus, one immediately—
The arising of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) corresponds to the four stages of application (*prayoga*) prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*).

From this point, one is able to induce the fundamental right gnosis (*mūla-samyagjñāna*), which is free from the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka*), and does not give rise to the marks of self, person, or phenomena (*ātma-pudgala-dharma-nimitta*). One thereby enters the first ground and continues up to the Buddha-ground;

although these are distinguished as partial or complete, they are not yet stable. In all cases, one personally realizes *tathatā* through fundamental non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). This is the ultimate refuge.
There is nothing to be attained. Why is this? That which is called the "characteristic of dharmas" (dharmalakṣaṇa) is something ordinary beings fail to understand; they take it to be real.
Yet, as the Tathāgata has taught, it is not a truly existent characteristic of dharmas, but is merely a conventional designation (prajñapti).

This is even more so when discussed from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), where there is pure, singular True Suchness (tathatā), all-pervasive and pure, leaving no room for anything else within it. Who, then, could act as the agent?
Regarding the dharmic characteristics of self and person: if one can truly observe in this way, then the self is no-self, and dharmas are no-dharmas.
Free from names and free from marks, one enters the samādhi of True Suchness (tathatā). Only then does one believe that the Buddhas of the ten directions are equal and pure;

that the real is no-reality, and the transformation is no-transformation. How, then, could there be any distinction between identity and difference? This is explained according to *śamatha* (calm abiding).
One contemplates concentration and wisdom to shatter the [notions of] self and dharmas, thereby severing doubts regarding identity and difference.

The twenty-sixth doubt states: "While it is true that the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) and the dharma body (dharmakāya) are neither identical nor different, the transformation body is ultimately devoid of intrinsic substance when it manifests.
How, then, could the Dharma it preaches possess any reality? Even if one were to uphold and preach it, there must be [some basis for its existence]."
"What is the merit?
Subhūti, if there were someone who, with the seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds, were to offer them as a gift;
and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon the bodhicitta and holds this sūtra, even for a moment..."
To receive, uphold, read, and recite even as little as four lines of a verse, and to expound them for others—this merit surpasses the former. How does one expound them for others?
Without grasping at signs, remaining unmoving in accordance with suchness (*tathatā*).

This section dispels doubts regarding the lack of merit in the teaching of the Dharma by the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The text has two parts. First, it clarifies the merit of teaching the Dharma. The *Śāstra* states:

"Although the activities of the various Buddhas’ transformation bodies include the teaching of the Dharma by the transformation body, which possesses immeasurable, inexhaustible, and untainted (*anāsrava*) merit...
[The passage continues with] "How can one expound it for others? and so forth. Second, it clarifies that the teaching of the Dharma is undefiled; that is to say, if one is able to remain unstained...

To expound the Dharma of the true nature (*dharmatā*) by means of a mind characterized by arising and ceasing is, in itself, like that *tathatā* (suchness); therefore, it is called "such-as-it-is" (*yathābhūta*).
Furthermore, because the mind is as suchness is, it is called "such-as-it-is. As for "immovable," this precisely clarifies the meaning of being undefiled. Wuzhuo says:
Because he preaches the Dharma without being defiled, there is such great benefit as this.

The twenty-seventh doubt asks: If this is so, then since the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata constantly preaches the Dharma for sentient beings, why is it said that the Tathāgata has no coming or going, sitting or reclining, and is eternally in *nirvāṇa*? *Nirvāṇa* is quiescent.
"Quiescence. Preaching the Dharma involves clamor and movement; movement and quiescence are opposites. How can both coexist? The meaning of the explanation is as follows:

The Buddha possesses wondrous wisdom, which contemplates all phenomena as empty, like dreams and illusions. Although he manifests the preaching of the Dharma, appearing to possess the characteristics of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*), he nonetheless abides eternally in the principle of nirvāṇa, which is non-active. How, then, can there be any doubt?
Why is this? One should contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) as being like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew, and likewise like lightning.
This addresses the doubt regarding how one who has entered cessation (*nirodha*) can preach the Dharma. The inquiry asks: For what reason does preaching the Dharma not obstruct nirvāṇa?

Vande. Because the Tathāgata possesses wondrous wisdom, he contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as being entirely without substantial reality, like dreams, illusions, and so forth.
There are six such metaphors. First is the metaphor of the dream: it refers to what is perfumed by the sights and sounds encountered during a person’s daily activities.
When one sleeps at night, these things appear vividly; amidst ten thousand forms of sorrow and joy, everyone regards them as real.

They do not know that these are transformations produced by the solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and possess no substantial reality whatsoever. Yet, whether good or bad, these objective realms are not non-existent while one is dreaming;
once one awakens, however, they are found to be utterly non-existent. Human life in this world is just like this: because of beginningless time...
It comes and dwells through habitual perfuming; therefore, it summons and brings about present retributions without fail.

Although the transformation of Zhuang Zhou into a butterfly represents the ultimate limit of change, how could he have realized that it was only empty after the fact? While his spirit was still wandering, the reality of the actual state had already been absent;

this is not something one waits to know only after awakening. Second, the analogy of illusion: In the world there is a master of illusions who performs magical arts; by means of incantations, he can [transform] a cloth...
One perceives a rabbit where there is only grass, or one mistakes it for a horse; or one fashions city walls, men, and women—various illusory forms that delude the ignorant.
Once the illusory spell ceases, all is silent and nothing remains. Third is the analogy of the bubble:

Water is inherently still, yet because it is stirred by the wind, bubbles arise. Their substance is fundamentally empty; upon examination, where do they abide? Fourth is the analogy of the reflection: A mirror... [text ends]
In the midst of day and night, images manifest according to their forms; beauty and ugliness leave nothing hidden. Movement and stillness depend on conditions;
one cannot grasp them, for they have no substance that can be apprehended. Only by resting in the shadow and awakening to the source may one hope not to be deluded by them.
Otherwise, one will forever walk beneath the shadow of a lamp. These four metaphors illustrate that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are empty and lack substantial reality. Ordinary beings—
All cling to the body and the world as permanent and fail to realize impermanence; therefore, the Buddha further taught the metaphor of the dew:

"How easily does the dew upon a scallion evaporate? A person’s dwelling in this world is but for a short time; it changes and perishes in an instant—how could it possibly endure long? Then he taught the metaphor of lightning:
"Even dew lingers for a brief moment, but lightning cannot remain for even a single blink of an eye; it arises and ceases simultaneously, never staying at all."
At another time [the Buddha said]: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are thus: they perish in every moment (*kṣaṇa-bhaṅga*), yet people do not perceive this themselves.

The Buddha, through his wondrous wisdom, contemplates emptiness; therefore, although he manifests the teaching of the Dharma with what appear to be conditioned characteristics, he abides eternally in the principle of nirvāṇa, which is unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*).
This is what is meant by being 'silent and solitary within the realm of myriad transformations, while active and functioning within the midst of the single void.'"
What distinction can there be between clamor and stillness? Thus it is said: "Like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow—the principle of emptiness is fully revealed.

Through the two metaphors of dew and lightning, impermanence is sufficiently manifested. To realize true emptiness is to not dwell in any phenomena; to contemplate arising and ceasing is to exhort one's practice.

This perfectly accords with the school that shatters forms and skillfully demonstrates the contemplation of the extinction of deluded emotions. If one thoroughly understands these six metaphors, then...
The essential purport of the entire sutra has been largely considered herein. Students should apply their minds to it with utmost diligence. The Section on the True Teaching is concluded.
III. The Section on Dissemination.
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Elder Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [and upāsikās...]
The upāsikā, all the world, including devas, humans, and asuras, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced;
they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The essential tenets have now been set forth above, with the aim of benefiting and delivering others.

This shall provide immediate benefit for those present at this assembly and reach far into the future to inspire those who are yet to come, ensuring that the life-force of Prajñā-wisdom is transmitted without obstruction; thus it is called "circulation" (liutong).
Furthermore, while the ultimate goal of the Prajñā school is the nirvana of non-abiding, it takes the arousal of the bodhicitta as its beginning. The bodhi-...
The "lifting of the mind" refers to the fundamentally original, intrinsically pure mind. When the mind dwells upon phenomena, it is no longer pure;

therefore, it does not dwell on the four marks, nor does it dwell on the six sense objects. It does not dwell on the fruits of the śrāvaka’s own attainment, nor does it dwell on the bodhisattva’s adornment of buddha-lands, nor even on the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks. It does not dwell even upon the preaching of the Dharma.
Nirvana does not abide; that which should abide is the ultimate realization of non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*).
In the preceding section on the True Doctrine, when Subhūti had questions, the Buddha provided answers; when Subhūti had doubts, the Buddha offered resolutions.
Now, the sun of wisdom shines in the sky, and all doubts are dissolved like melting ice. Subhūti has no further questions, and the Capable One [the Buddha] ceases his proclamation. Elder [Subhūti].

Subhūti, as well as all the fourfold assembly of disciples—those who have left the household life as *bhikṣus* (almsmen) and *bhikṣuṇīs* (almswomen), and those who remain at home as *upāsakas* (laymen of pure faith) and *upāsikās* (laywomen)—and even all the world, including the three realms of existence:
whether they be devas, Brahmā kings, Śakras, or others; whether they be humans, such as kings, ministers, or elders; [all are included].

O noble ones, if the asuras, the eight classes of protectors of the Dharma, and others are all present within this assembly and hear the Prajñāpāramitā taught by the Buddha, they will each rejoice and practice it accordingly.
An ancient master said: "The profound sūtras of Prajñā are the Mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

By hearing even a single four-line verse of these sūtras, one transcends the causes for rebirth in the evil realms; by maintaining them with pure mindfulness for even a single thought-moment, one will certainly attain [enlightenment]."
This is the fruit of Bodhi. Therefore, those who wish to perfect the path to unsurpassed Bodhi should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
The Ancient Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Sūtra concludes here.
